newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-WILDERNESS YEARS NOW JUST A MEMORY FOR LEIGHTON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WILDERNESS YEARS NOW JUST A MEMORY FOR LEIGHTON.

text.p: Jim Leighton lost a proud record in Gothenburg on Wednesday night.
But more importantly he retained the hard-won respect of his fellow players and fans, in a career which began at Aberdeen in the 1978-79 season.

Before Wednesday the 38-year-old Scotland goalkeeper had last conceded a tournament goal in 1990. That run ended when Kennet Andersson scored both of Sweden's goals in their 2-1 World Cup qualifier in the Ullevi Stadium.

Brazilian striker Muller was the last player to score against Leighton in a competitive international during the 1990 World Cup finals, a goal which brought down the curtain on the first half of Leighton's international career.
After that 1-0 defeat in Turin, which eliminated Scotland from Italia '90, Leighton did not play another international until November 1993.
But now his rehabilitation is complete. He won his 78th cap on Wednesday to become Scotland's second most-capped player behind Kenny Dalglish, who played for his country 102 times.
Leighton's comeback is a remarkable story of self-belief and fortitude.
And as a measure of his renewed standing his first club, Aberdeen, whom he helped establish as one of Europe's top clubs in the mid-1980s, are set to lure him back home from Hibernian this year..
In hindsight, he probably should never have left the oil city nine years ago to follow his mentor Alex Ferguson to Manchester United.

Ferguson spent 650,000 pounds sterling ($1.1 million) in 1988 on the 'keeper who had helped him win the European Cup Winners' Cup, the European Super Cup and three Scottish championships with Aberdeen.

But the relationship between the pair men degenerated at Old Trafford and the manager prompted Leighton's years in the doldrums by dropping him from the F.A. Cup final replay with Crystal Palace in 1990 after mistakes in the original 3-3 draw.
"Alex was always ruthless when it came to football,' Leighton reflected. "And I knew our past together was not going to help me.
"If he has to make a decision for the good of the team, no matter how unpopular it is, he makes it. I suppose he was vindicated because United won the cup without me in the replay."

Leighton's confidence, already badly dented, was about to be crushed. Four weeks later he conceded the only goal when Costa Rica humbled Scotland 1-0 in the World Cup finals and although they recovered to beat Sweden, he had a nightmare in Turin when Brazil beat Scotland 1-0 to knock them out of the competition.

Leighton found himself in exile for three years, unable to get a game for Manchester United's second team and loaned to Reading, Sheffield United and Dundee before former Hibernian manager Alex Miller, the assistant to national coach Craig Brown, threw him a lifeline.
Hibs signed him in July 1993, his confidence was gradually restored and now he is back at the very top.
He chooses not to dwell on those years, but does concede: "In hindsight, perhaps it was wrong to go to Manchester United. I had offers at the time to go abroad -- but you can't turn United down."
Leighton's first cap came in 1983 against East Germany at the height of Aberdeen's success.
"I was lucky because I had my club's central defenders Willie Miller and Alex McLeish in front of me for Scotland too and we had a great understanding.
"I gained a lot of great experience with Aberdeen because we were one of the best teams in Europe then.
"Winning the Cup Winners' Cup by beating Real Madrid in Gothenburg will always be my top memory -- thats why it was nice to get my 78th cap in the same city."

Leighton came close to severing his ties with Scotland last year after being chosen as deputy to Rangers' Andy Goram for the Euro' 96 finals in England after playing in six and making one brief substitute appearance in the seventh of the 10 qualifiers.
"I was very upset and it took me the whole summer to get over it," he said.
"I was going to give up international football for good, but my wife talked me out of it and I'm glad she did."
Despite Wednesday's defeat, Scotland are still very much on course for the finals in France next year. If he plays, they would be his third World Cup finals.
"I feel I could go on for a while yet, maybe even till I'm 42, so hopefully there are a few more major tournaments left for me yet."
